reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: The most common inherited disorder of mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation, caused by deficiency of medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase
Classically presents in infancy or early childhood with hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and lethargy or coma precipitated by fasting or an intercurrent illness
Vomiting, hepatomegaly and encephalopathy may accompany crises, and sudden unexpected death can occur, sometimes mimicking sudden infant death syndrome
The key clue is inappropriately low or absent ketones despite hypoglycaemia, since fat cannot be used as fuel during fasting
The acylcarnitine profile shows elevated medium-chain species (notably octanoylcarnitine, C8) with a raised C8:C10 ratio, and urine shows medium-chain dicarboxylic aciduria
Between episodes children are typically well, and the disorder can be clinically silent until a catabolic stress unmasks it
Management is essentially preventive: avoidance of fasting, prompt provision of glucose during illness, and an emergency regimen, with generally no need for severe dietary fat restriction
Now widely detected on newborn screening by elevated C8 acylcarnitine, which has markedly reduced deaths from unrecognised disease
reference.pathophysiology: MCAD deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder, usually due to a common ACADM gene variant, that impairs the beta-oxidation of medium-chain fatty acids. During fasting the body normally shifts to oxidising fatty acids for energy and generating ketones for the brain; when medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase is deficient, this pathway stalls, so energy production fails and ketogenesis is inadequate. Glucose is consumed without adequate fat-derived backup, producing hypoketotic hypoglycaemia. Accumulated medium-chain fatty acids and their carnitine and glycine conjugates are toxic and contribute to encephalopathy and hepatic dysfunction. Secondary carnitine depletion is common.
additionalDifferentials: Other fatty acid oxidation defects (LCHAD, VLCAD, carnitine transport/CPT defects)
Ketotic hypoglycaemia and other causes of childhood hypoglycaemia
Sepsis and sudden unexpected death in infancy
additionalInvestigations: Blood glucose, ketones (inappropriately low), and blood gas during an episode
Plasma acylcarnitine profile (elevated C8 with raised C8:C10 ratio)
Urine organic acids showing medium-chain dicarboxylic aciduria
Plasma free and total carnitine (often low)
Molecular testing of the ACADM gene
redFlags: Hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with encephalopathy or coma during fasting or illness is a life-threatening emergency
Sudden collapse or unexpected death, particularly in a previously well infant
Prolonged fasting, vomiting or poor intake during intercurrent illness without glucose provision
First presentation of an undiagnosed child with unexplained hypoglycaemic coma
reference.prognosis: With diagnosis (especially via newborn screening) and simple preventive measures the prognosis is excellent and most individuals remain healthy; however, an unrecognised metabolic crisis can cause sudden death or permanent neurological injury, so the main determinant of outcome is prevention of fasting-induced decompensation.
pitfalls: Overlooking the disorder because the child is entirely well between episodes
Failing to recognise that ketones are inappropriately low for the degree of hypoglycaemia
Not providing an emergency glucose plan for periods of illness or fasting
Assuming SIDS in an infant death without considering an underlying fatty acid oxidation defect
management: Avoid prolonged fasting with regular carbohydrate-containing feeds as the cornerstone of prevention
Provide an emergency regimen for intercurrent illness, escalating to intravenous dextrose to reverse catabolism and prevent hypoketotic hypoglycaemia
Avoid medium-chain triglyceride oil, which bypasses the enzymatic block and can precipitate crises
Consider L-carnitine supplementation where secondary carnitine deficiency is documented
Manage acute metabolic decompensation urgently with intravenous glucose and correction of hypoglycaemia and encephalopathy
Identify cases early through newborn screening and involve a metabolic specialist and dietitian
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance and test at-risk siblings
Provide a written emergency care plan and family education, as unrecognised crises can be fatal
